items.item: the set of replicas is collectively a Paxos group
the key enabler of Spanner's properties is a new TrueTime API and its implementation
Spanner is the first system to provide external-consistency guarantees at global scale
running two-phase commit over Paxos mitigates the availability problems general two-phase commit otherwise brings
CockroachDB stores all user data in a sorted map of key-value pairs, divided into contiguous ranges
CockroachDB uses the Raft consensus protocol; a quorum of nodes containing replicas of a range acknowledge each write
CockroachDB implements hybrid-logical clocks, composed of a physical and a logical component, to optimize read performance

sources.source: Concurrency control in Aurora DSQL (AWS documentation)

items.item: Aurora DSQL uses optimistic concurrency control, evaluating conflicts at commit time instead of using locks
under Aurora DSQL's OCC, the transaction with the earliest commit time succeeds and the conflicting transaction receives an OC000 response

The Spanner pattern's own novelty wasn't inventing a new mechanism — it was proving that range-sharding, per-range consensus, and two-phase commit could compose into one system at global scale without one mechanism breaking another's own guarantees.

A hybrid logical clock's logical component only ever advances; it never resets, because resetting it the moment the physical clock catches up would let two causally-ordered events tie or invert, which is exactly the property the logical component exists to prevent.

at.step: Reveal: a clock that never goes backward

items.item: Commit wait's cost is paid once per commit, not once per read — a read-only transaction in Spanner's own design can avoid the wait entirely by reading at a safe, already-passed timestamp, which this topic's own reveal doesn't build out but names as the reason read-heavy workloads pay this cost far less than write-heavy ones.

Optimistic concurrency control isn't free of coordination — it moves the coordination from before the work (a lock) to after it (a commit-time check); the real trade is whether wasted work from a late-discovered conflict is cheaper than blocking every transaction upfront, which depends entirely on how often transactions actually collide.

TiDB and YugabyteDB are named alongside CockroachDB because both document the identical range-sharded-keyspace-plus-per-range-consensus architecture Spanner popularized, not because they're interchangeable in every other respect — this topic names the shared pattern, not every implementation difference between the three.

Aurora DSQL's May 2025 GA matters to this topic's own scope specifically because it's documented as a genuinely different trade (optimistic, commit-time-only checks) rather than a reimplementation of the Spanner pattern under a new name — the syllabus's own framing ('Aurora DSQL's alternative') is accurate, not marketing.

The round-trip cost this topic measures for a cross-range commit is a floor, not a ceiling — real systems add retries, network variance, and (for Spanner specifically) the commit-wait window on top of the bare consensus-plus-2PC round trips counted here.

Choosing 'shard a boring Postgres' over a distributed SQL system isn't a admission of lesser engineering — every one of this topic's own measured costs exists to solve a problem (data spread across machines) that a dataset fitting on one machine simply doesn't have.

This topic's own executable claims model commit wait and HLC timestamps as unitless integers rather than real wall-clock milliseconds, specifically to keep the ordering claim (strictly increasing, respects real-time causality) checkable and deterministic without depending on this sandbox's own clock behavior.

This topic's own 'Prove it' answer generalizes a theme running through this entire chapter's tail (topics 19 through 24): every coordination mechanism measured here pays a real, non-zero cost, and the right engineering call is whichever side of that cost a given workload's actual needs land on, not a default toward 'more distributed is better.'
